video_title: Ready For A Bear Market? Most Investors Aren't | Ted Oakley @OxbowAdvisors
gist: Oxbow Advisors' Ted Oakley calls the US economy an AI 'one-trick pony' and warns that the top 10–12 companies, about 41–42% of the S&P 500, could produce a dot-com-sized bear market that index investors, inexperienced advisors and equity-heavy baby boomers are not ready for. Meanwhile Oxbow holds a lot of liquidity, overweights energy (about 15–17% including pipelines) and materials/miners as the cheapest sectors, and stays in 3–18-month Treasuries. Oakley says he would only trade the long bond once oil rolls over and stops driving inflation.

insights.claim: Ted Oakley calls the US economy a 'one-trick pony' tied to AI: strip out the AI build-out and the growth numbers would be far weaker, and he says the build-out will pass in time. The host puts Q3 GDPNow above 5% even with the Fed hiking and the 10-year Treasury near 5.1%.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Headline US growth depends heavily on AI capex, so any slowdown in the build-out would hit GDP and earnings together.
insights.quote: because the economy, it's a one-trick pony.

insights.claim: Oakley says the average of the S&P 500's 11 sectors is down about 18–19% from its high, even though the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) looks fine, so the broad market is weaker than the cap-weighted indexes suggest.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Narrow leadership is hiding a stealth bear market in the average sector, and cap-weighted index strength overstates market health.

insights.claim: Oakley contrasts today with 1999–2000, when only telecom and tech were bubbling and everything else was cheap (Oxbow made good money in the 2000–2003 bear market by owning cheap stocks). Now companies in every sector, including banks, utilities and industrials, are tying their story to AI.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: The usual rotation into 'cheap old economy' stocks may protect less in an AI unwind, because AI narratives have been priced into many sectors.

insights.claim: Oakley says his numbers show projected AI profitability over the next two to three years is nowhere near what is being promised, so the chance of it not working out is fairly high, and he adds that many of these companies carry a lot of debt while promising large profits.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Leveraged AI spenders are the most exposed if returns disappoint; watch AI capex ROI and credit spreads on AI-linked debt.

insights.claim: Oakley expects an AI-driven bear market to be about as bad as the dot-com bust because the top 10–12 companies, about 41–42% of the S&P 500, control the index averages, so passive index holders are far less diversified than they think.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Passive S&P 500 exposure is effectively a concentrated AI bet; equal-weight or active diversification is the hedge.
insights.quote: You got to remember if you own the index, you're not very diversified.

insights.claim: Oakley expects that within 12–18 months investors may realize AI companies are not nearly as profitable as expected and sell, causing fairly big corrective moves; he does not think today's concentration in AI names will last over the next year or two.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: This gives a rough 2027 window for an AI earnings-reality correction; Oxbow deliberately avoids names like Nvidia.

insights.claim: Oakley sees a possible good long-run outcome from AI, like the internet after 2000: price competition, including Chinese AI produced at roughly 4% of US cost, makes AI cheaper and more productive, while the companies promising outsized profits disappoint.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Low-cost Chinese competition could commoditize AI: good for AI users' productivity, bad for AI providers' margins and valuations.

insights.claim: Oakley says energy has been the number one performing sector this year yet is ignored and underowned. It was about 3% of the S&P 500 at the start of the year, while Oxbow holds about 15% (about 17% including pipelines) and says the sector is still really cheap with the best dividends.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: An underowned, cheap, high-dividend energy sector with momentum makes a contrarian overweight, and a diversifier against AI concentration.
insights.quote: they really leave money on the table when it comes to energy.

insights.claim: Oakley names materials (miners, including gold miners, plus copper, silver, aluminum and iron) and energy (producers, service companies and pipelines) as Oxbow's two top sectors and the cheapest areas to concentrate in now.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: A value manager is positioning in real-asset sectors as the cheapest part of the market, a hedge against an AI-led drawdown.

insights.claim: Oakley describes an energy-cycle sequence: oil leads, natural gas follows, and oil service companies come last. He says gas stocks are now coming alive, and Oxbow owns the whole chain including Schlumberger, Transocean, Noble, NESR (mostly Middle East business) and some coal.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: If gas is inflecting now, the framework points to oil services (SLB, offshore drillers) as the next leg of the energy rotation.

insights.claim: Oakley says commodity and energy holdings are mostly insulated from AI hype, apart from demand for inputs like copper, aluminum and silver, which makes them a diversifier against an AI unwind.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Raw commodities give AI-adjacent demand exposure without paying AI-narrative valuations.

insights.claim: Oakley says countries have become hoarders of critical minerals rather than trading them, citing tungsten: Oxbow owns it, but there is only one really good US-listed tungsten company and the rest of supply is overseas and not being shared.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Resource nationalism raises the scarcity value of domestic critical-mineral producers, especially rare US-listed pure plays like tungsten.
insights.quote: I'm going to keep what I have. I'm not going to trade it with you.

insights.claim: Oakley argues pipelines are close to monopolies because new long-haul lines, such as a 2,000-mile pipeline, can't get easements and states will block them; he doubts the president can revive Keystone. Oxbow rarely sells its pipelines because of their high cash flows paid on K-1s.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Permitting barriers protect existing midstream assets' pricing power and volume-based cash flow, a long-duration income hold.

insights.claim: Oakley says Oxbow owns Union Pacific and that its merger with Norfolk Southern will create an ocean-to-ocean railroad that cannot be replicated, because no one can get the easements to build another.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: A combined UNP-NSC transcontinental network would be an irreplaceable moat asset, the same logic as pipelines.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart argues midstream companies face a development boom: the US is now the world's largest oil exporter and is raising output because of the Iran war, buyers and Gulf producers are rerouting oil (including via pipelines to the Red Sea), and a new 100-year US deal on Venezuelan oil will need infrastructure. Oakley agrees this benefits midstream.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart / Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Supply-chain rerouting away from the Gulf and Venezuela buildout are tailwinds for US midstream and oilfield-services firms.

themes.theme: Short Treasuries, oil and the long bond

insights.claim: Oxbow keeps fixed income in 3-month to 3-year Treasuries, mostly 6-, 9-, 12-, 15- and 18-month bills and notes, so it can 'define the outcome' by holding to maturity; Oakley says long-term bond funds have lost money since 2020 and holders can't get out.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Short bills held to maturity avoid mark-to-market losses on duration while still capturing yields in the mid-4s.
insights.quote: the key to it is you have to define the limits of when you're going to get that money back.

insights.claim: Oakley cites the 2-year Treasury at 4.65% versus the 30-year at 5.08%, arguing that roughly 43 basis points of extra yield doesn't justify long duration risk.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: The flat 2s30s term premium favors the front end over long bonds until the inflation driver turns.
insights.quote: why would I buy a a 30-year at 508 when I get 465 for two years?

insights.claim: Oakley says oil is the driver of the CPI problem through diesel, gasoline, food and building costs. He thinks oil has further to go, and only once it rolls over will a one-to-two-year long-bond trade open up, which he doesn't expect in the next few quarters.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Use an oil price rollover as the trigger to add duration; until then, avoid the long end.
insights.quote: eventually that I think oil will tame the interest rates.

insights.claim: Oakley notes oil can reverse violently, going from $140 in 2008 to $38 about six months later, and says a soft US economy in 2027 could line up with oil to create a long-bond rally.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: A 2027 slowdown is a possible catalyst for lower long yields once oil breaks.

insights.claim: Oakley says Oxbow made more money in the long bond from 2018 to March–April 2020 with a 7–8% position than ever before, as rates went to nothing, but later attempts to trade it failed, and many investors trading the long bond since have been hurt as prices kept falling.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Long bonds only pay in a clear disinflation or crisis regime; in an inflation regime they are a trap.

insights.claim: Oakley says the US is running 6% deficits outside a recession, the current administration is spending as much as its predecessors, and debt growing about 7.2% a year would require roughly 15% economic growth to make it work.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Structural deficits keep upward pressure on Treasury supply and yields regardless of Fed policy.
insights.quote: we're running 6% deficits that that that has to stop at some point

insights.claim: US national debt has roughly doubled since 2016 (Oakley) and has gone from about $8 trillion before the 2008 crisis to $40 trillion now, more than quadrupling in under 20 years (Taggart).
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Debt growth is a secular headwind for long-duration Treasuries and a support for hard assets.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart argues the administration is trying to 'run the economy hot' to improve the debt-to-GDP ratio, citing Q3 GDP above 5%, but says its sustainability is uncertain if the AI sector falters; Oakley agrees a hotter economy is one lever but insists spending must be cut.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart / Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: A run-it-hot policy implies sticky inflation and higher nominal yields, and it depends on AI capex staying strong.

insights.claim: Oakley notes that in the 1970s and 1980s tough bear markets came every four to five years, and in the 1970s almost every other year, and warns investors that the Fed can't bail them out now, since an intervention would only make things worse.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Don't count on a Fed put in an inflationary, high-debt regime; position for longer, deeper drawdowns than recent history suggests.
insights.quote: they have to remember that the Fed can't bail them out now.

insights.claim: Oakley expects that many advisors who have never managed through a bear market will ride losses down, as with the Nasdaq's roughly 80% fall after 2000, and capitulate near the lows. He says the industry is all in with little liquidity, and that is when investors holding cash can do their best ever.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Keeping dry powder is the edge: forced capitulation by under-experienced managers creates the entry point.

insights.claim: Oakley says Oxbow's best years all came out of bear markets (1987–88, 2003, 2009), including buying stocks in Q1 2009 that paid 15% dividends, which is why the firm always keeps some liquidity and carries a lot now.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: The payoff from holding cash comes after a bear market, when yields on quality stocks spike.

insights.claim: Oakley expects the next ten years or so to resemble the 1930s–40s: a weak era overall with periods where investors who have liquidity and reliquify do well. The host says Oakley is not calling an imminent bear market.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: Expect a low-return decade with tradeable drawdowns, and favor a barbell of cash plus cheap cash-flowing assets over buy-and-hold indexing.

insights.claim: Baby boomers have the highest equity exposure of any cohort: Oakley sees 65-year-olds about to retire with 90% in stocks, 80-year-olds at 80–90%, and an 84-year-old at 95%, while the average boomer has about $1.6 million and the median only $500–600K.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: The oldest investors have the most equity risk and the least time to recover, a forced-seller cohort in any deep bear market.

insights.claim: Oakley's cash-flow framework: if holdings yield 8–10% in cash, you don't have to be very good to average 15% over five years; Oxbow holds positions yielding 5–12%, including oil and gas royalty company Kimbell Royalty at about 11.2%.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: High-yield energy royalties do much of the work toward a return target, which reduces the need for equity beta.

insights.claim: Oakley says Oxbow's stock portfolio of about 45 companies (the high-income portfolio holds about 30) includes growth names such as a recent purchase of Ferrari and many foreign companies that are cheap on price-to-cash-flow.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: A disciplined value manager finds cheaper growth outside US AI mega-caps, including in luxury and foreign stocks.
insights.quote: we just bought Ferrari over there.

insights.claim: Oakley says Oxbow's high-income accounts target about 3–4 points over inflation and have beaten that over the past four to five years, and that the firm will lag the S&P 500 in up years because it holds more cash but outperforms in down years.
insights.speaker: Ted Oakley
insights.so_what: An inflation-plus-3–4% target is a realistic benchmark for capital-preservation income portfolios in this regime.
